title: Current State Assessment: Understanding What You're Working With
objectives: Map existing systems and their relationships accurately
Assess technical debt honestly and communicate it effectively
Identify and document integration points and dependencies
Distinguish between pain points and their root causes
Produce current state documentation that enables good decision-making
whyThisMatters:
You cannot design a good future state without understanding the current state. This sounds obvious, but it's remarkable how often architects skip this step — or do it superficially — because they're eager to start designing the new solution. In government, where systems have accumulated over decades and institutional knowledge has been lost as people moved on, understanding the current state is both more difficult and more important than in most other contexts.

The current state isn't just a list of systems. It's the web of relationships between systems, the data that flows between them, the processes that depend on them, the contracts that govern them, and the people who operate them. Miss any of these dimensions and your future state design will have blind spots that become expensive surprises during delivery.

content.heading: Why Current State Assessment Matters
content.body:
Every architecture project starts from somewhere. Even a completely new service exists within a landscape of existing systems, data sources, processes, and organisational structures. Understanding this landscape is essential for several reasons.

**Integration reality.** Your new service will need to connect to existing systems. If you don't understand those systems — their capabilities, their limitations, their interfaces — you'll design integrations that don't work. The most common cause of government IT project delays is integration with legacy systems that behave differently from how they were documented (or weren't documented at all).

**Data reality.** Your new service will need data that currently lives somewhere else. If you don't understand the current data landscape — where data is, what format it's in, how reliable it is, who owns it — you'll make assumptions about data availability that turn out to be wrong.

**Process reality.** Your new service will change how people work. If you don't understand the current processes — including the workarounds, the exceptions, and the informal practices that keep things running — you'll design a service that breaks existing workflows without providing adequate replacements.

**Political reality.** Existing systems have owners, supporters, and defenders. If you don't understand the organisational dynamics around current systems, you'll encounter resistance that you didn't anticipate. The team that built the current system may see your project as a criticism of their work. The vendor that supports it may see your project as a threat to their contract.

**Cost reality.** Understanding the current state helps you estimate the true cost of change. Migration costs, data cleansing costs, training costs, parallel running costs, decommissioning costs — these are all determined by the current state and are frequently underestimated because the current state wasn't properly understood.

A thorough current state assessment isn't a luxury — it's a risk mitigation activity. Every hour you spend understanding the current state saves multiple hours of rework, troubleshooting, and crisis management during delivery.

content.heading: Mapping Existing Systems
content.body:
System mapping is the foundation of current state assessment. The goal is to create a clear picture of what systems exist, what they do, how they connect, and who depends on them.

**Start with what's known.** Review existing documentation — architecture diagrams, system registers, CMDB entries, contract documents. But treat this documentation with healthy scepticism. In government, documentation is frequently out of date. Systems have been modified without updating the docs. Integrations have been added informally. Components have been decommissioned on paper but not in practice.

**Validate through interviews.** Talk to the people who actually use and operate the systems. They know the reality that documentation misses. Ask: 'What systems do you use daily?' 'What data do you get from other systems?' 'What manual processes fill gaps between systems?' 'What breaks most often?'

**Map the connections.** For each system, identify: what data flows in and out, what other systems it connects to, what protocols and interfaces are used, and how frequently data is exchanged. Pay special attention to informal connections — the spreadsheet that someone downloads from System A and uploads to System B every Monday morning is an integration, even if it's not automated.

**Assess the health.** For each system, assess: Is it actively maintained? When was it last updated? Is the technology still supported? Are there known security vulnerabilities? Is the vendor still in business? Is the source code available? These health indicators help you understand the risk profile of each system.

**Document the dependencies.** Create a dependency map showing which systems depend on which others. This reveals the critical path — the systems whose failure would cascade through the landscape. It also reveals the integration complexity you'll face when making changes.

A practical tip: use a simple, visual format for your system map. A complex diagram that requires specialist tools to read is less useful than a clear whiteboard sketch that everyone can understand. The goal is shared understanding, not architectural art.

In government, you'll often discover systems that nobody knew about — a database running on someone's desktop, a scheduled task on a server that nobody remembers setting up, a third-party service that a previous team subscribed to. These shadow systems are important because they represent unmet needs that your new solution may need to address.

content.heading: Understanding Technical Debt
content.body:
Technical debt is the accumulated cost of past decisions that were expedient at the time but create ongoing burden. In government, technical debt is pervasive and often poorly understood. As an architect, you need to assess it honestly and communicate it effectively.

**Types of technical debt in government systems:**

*Deliberate debt:* Decisions made consciously to meet a deadline or budget constraint. 'We'll hard-code the business rules for now and make them configurable later.' This debt is manageable if it's documented and there's a plan to address it. In practice, 'later' often never comes.

*Accidental debt:* Debt that accumulated without anyone noticing. The codebase grew organically, patterns diverged, dependencies became tangled. This is common in systems maintained by rotating teams of contractors who each brought their own preferences.

*Environmental debt:* Debt caused by changes in the external environment. The technology was current when chosen but is now obsolete. The security standards have changed. The vendor has been acquired and the product roadmap has shifted. This type of debt is inevitable and not anyone's fault.

*Knowledge debt:* The people who understood the system have left, and their knowledge wasn't captured. This is particularly acute in government, where civil servants rotate frequently and contractor engagements end. A system that nobody fully understands is a system that's expensive and risky to change.

**Assessing technical debt:**

Don't try to quantify all technical debt — that's an endless exercise. Instead, focus on the debt that affects your project:

- What debt will make integration harder? (Outdated APIs, undocumented interfaces, fragile data formats)
- What debt will make migration harder? (Poor data quality, missing data, inconsistent data models)
- What debt will make operation harder? (Missing monitoring, manual deployment processes, undocumented configuration)
- What debt creates security risk? (Unpatched systems, unsupported software, weak authentication)

**Communicating technical debt:**

Technical debt is a concept that non-technical stakeholders struggle with. Use analogies they understand: 'This system is like a building where maintenance has been deferred for years. It still stands, but every repair is more expensive than it should be because you have to work around the accumulated problems.' Quantify where you can: 'Every change to this system takes three times longer than it should because of the accumulated complexity.' Connect debt to business impact: 'This technical debt means we can't respond to policy changes within the required timeframe.'

content.heading: Assessing Integration Points
content.body:
Integration points are where systems meet — and where projects most commonly fail. A thorough assessment of existing integration points is essential for any architecture project that involves changing or replacing systems.

For each integration point, assess:

**Interface type:** Is it an API (REST, SOAP, GraphQL)? A file transfer (SFTP, S3)? A database link? A message queue? A manual process (someone copying data between systems)? The interface type determines the complexity and risk of changing the integration.

**Data exchanged:** What data flows across this integration? What format is it in? How is it validated? What happens when invalid data is received? Understanding the data contract is essential — changing it affects both sides of the integration.

**Frequency and volume:** Is data exchanged in real-time, near-real-time, or batch? How much data flows per exchange? What's the peak volume? These characteristics shape the integration architecture for the future state.

**Reliability:** How often does this integration fail? What happens when it fails? Is there retry logic? Is there a dead letter queue? Is there manual intervention? Unreliable integrations are a major source of operational pain and need to be addressed in the future state design.

**Ownership:** Who owns each side of the integration? Who is responsible for maintaining it? Who needs to be involved if it changes? In government, integration ownership is often unclear — the integration was built by a contractor who has since left, and neither team considers it 'theirs.'

**Contractual constraints:** Is the integration governed by a contract or service level agreement? Are there costs associated with changing it? Are there notice periods? In government, vendor contracts can significantly constrain your ability to change integrations.

**Documentation:** Is the integration documented? Is the documentation accurate? Can you find the API specification, the data dictionary, the error handling rules? Undocumented integrations are the highest-risk items in any current state assessment.

A practical approach: create an integration matrix showing every system-to-system connection, with columns for each of the assessment criteria above. This gives you a single view of the integration landscape and highlights the highest-risk integration points that need the most attention in your future state design.

content.heading: Documenting Current State Honestly
content.body:
Current state documentation serves a specific purpose: it enables good decision-making about the future state. This means it needs to be honest, even when honesty is uncomfortable.

**Common dishonesty patterns in current state documentation:**

*The optimistic assessment:* Describing systems as better than they are because the team that built them is still around and might be offended. 'The system has some minor data quality issues' when the reality is 'the data is so unreliable that the operations team maintains a parallel spreadsheet.'

*The blame-free assessment:* Describing problems without identifying causes because identifying causes might point to specific decisions or people. 'The system has accumulated technical debt' without explaining that the debt was caused by a procurement decision that prioritised lowest cost over quality.

*The scope-limited assessment:* Only documenting the systems within your project scope, ignoring the wider landscape that affects your project. Your new service might depend on a system that's outside your scope but is about to be decommissioned — if you don't document this, you'll discover it too late.

*The documentation-as-reality assessment:* Describing systems as they're documented rather than as they actually work. The architecture diagram shows a clean, well-structured system. The reality is a tangle of workarounds, patches, and undocumented modifications.

**What honest current state documentation looks like:**

It describes what actually exists, not what should exist. It identifies problems clearly, with evidence. It acknowledges uncertainty — 'we believe this system handles X, but we haven't been able to verify this because the documentation is incomplete.' It includes the informal systems and processes that keep things running. It assesses risk honestly — 'this system is a single point of failure with no disaster recovery capability.'

Honest documentation can be politically sensitive. The team that built the current system may feel criticised. The programme that funded it may feel their investment is being questioned. Handle this with care — focus on facts and evidence, not judgments. 'The system was built in 2015 using technology that was current at the time but is now end-of-life' is factual. 'The system was poorly designed' is a judgment that will create enemies.

The audience for current state documentation includes future architects who will inherit your work. Write for them. They need to understand not just what exists but why it exists, what works, what doesn't, and what risks they need to manage.

content.heading: Capability Mapping
content.body:
Capability mapping goes beyond system mapping to understand what the organisation can do — and what it can't. A capability is a combination of people, process, and technology that enables the organisation to achieve an outcome.

For example, 'process grant applications' is a capability that involves: caseworkers (people), the assessment process (process), and the grant management system (technology). Understanding the capability — not just the system — gives you a richer picture of the current state.

**Why capability mapping matters for architects:**

When you replace a system, you're not just replacing technology — you're changing a capability. If you only understand the technology dimension, you'll miss the people and process changes that are equally important. A new system that's technically superior but requires skills the team doesn't have, or supports a process that doesn't match how work actually gets done, will fail.

**How to create a capability map:**

1. Identify the key capabilities the organisation needs (e.g., 'receive applications,' 'assess eligibility,' 'make payments,' 'produce reports').
2. For each capability, document: what people are involved, what process they follow, what technology they use, and how well the capability performs.
3. Assess each capability: Is it meeting the organisation's needs? Where are the gaps? What's the maturity level?
4. Identify dependencies between capabilities — which capabilities depend on others?

**Capability maturity assessment:**

A simple maturity model helps communicate the current state to non-technical stakeholders:

- Level 1 (Ad hoc): The capability exists but is informal, inconsistent, and person-dependent.
- Level 2 (Managed): The capability has defined processes but relies heavily on manual effort.
- Level 3 (Standardised): The capability is consistent, documented, and supported by appropriate technology.
- Level 4 (Optimised): The capability is continuously improved based on data and feedback.

Most government capabilities sit at Level 1 or 2. Understanding this helps set realistic expectations for the future state — jumping from Level 1 to Level 4 in a single project is unrealistic. A more achievable goal might be moving from Level 1 to Level 2 or 3, with a roadmap for further improvement.

Capability mapping also reveals opportunities for reuse. If two teams have similar capabilities supported by different systems, there may be an opportunity to consolidate. But be careful — similar-looking capabilities often have important differences that only become apparent when you examine them closely.

content.heading: Identifying Pain Points vs Symptoms
content.body:
When you talk to people about the current state, they'll tell you about their pain points. But pain points are often symptoms of deeper problems, and treating symptoms without addressing causes is a recipe for expensive failure.

**Common symptom-cause patterns in government:**

*Symptom:* 'The system is too slow.'
*Possible causes:* The database queries are inefficient. The infrastructure is undersized. The network connection to the data centre is saturated. The system is doing unnecessary work. Users are running reports during peak transaction times.

*Symptom:* 'We can't get the data we need.'
*Possible causes:* The data exists but isn't accessible (permissions issue). The data exists but isn't in a usable format (data quality issue). The data doesn't exist (data collection gap). The data exists in another department but there's no sharing agreement (governance issue).

*Symptom:* 'The system doesn't do what we need.'
*Possible causes:* The requirements have changed since the system was built. The system was built to the wrong requirements. The system has the capability but users don't know how to use it. The system has the capability but it's buried in a poor user interface.

**How to distinguish symptoms from causes:**

Use the Five Whys technique (from Lesson 7) to trace symptoms to their root causes. For each pain point, ask: 'Why does this happen?' and keep asking until you reach a cause that, if addressed, would eliminate the symptom.

Also look for patterns. If multiple people report different symptoms that trace to the same root cause, that's a strong signal. If the operations team says 'the system is slow,' the users say 'the reports take too long,' and the developers say 'the database is a bottleneck,' they're all describing symptoms of the same cause — a data architecture that doesn't support the current usage patterns.

**Why this matters for architecture:**

If you design your future state to address symptoms rather than causes, you'll build a new system that has the same problems in different packaging. The new system will be fast initially (because it's new and the data volume is small) but will slow down as data accumulates — because you addressed the symptom (slow system) rather than the cause (poor data architecture).

Conversely, if you identify and address root causes, your future state design will be fundamentally better, not just superficially different. This is where the real value of current state assessment lies — not in cataloguing what exists, but in understanding why things are the way they are and what needs to change at a fundamental level.

content.heading: Producing Actionable Current State Documentation
content.body:
Current state documentation should drive action, not gather dust. Here's how to produce documentation that's genuinely useful.

**Structure for impact:**

1. **Executive summary** (1 page): The key findings that decision-makers need to know. What's the overall health of the current landscape? What are the biggest risks? What are the key constraints for the future state?

2. **System landscape** (2-3 pages): A visual map of the current systems and their connections, with a brief description of each system's purpose, technology, health, and owner.

3. **Integration assessment** (2-3 pages): The integration matrix showing all system-to-system connections with their characteristics and risk levels.

4. **Capability assessment** (2-3 pages): The capability map showing current maturity levels and gaps.

5. **Technical debt register** (1-2 pages): The significant technical debt items that affect the future state, with impact assessment and recommended approach.

6. **Risks and constraints** (1-2 pages): The risks and constraints that the future state design must address or work within.

7. **Recommendations** (1 page): What the current state assessment means for the future state approach. Not the design itself, but the principles and constraints that should guide it.

**Keep it visual.** Diagrams communicate more effectively than text for system landscapes and integration maps. Use consistent notation and keep diagrams simple enough to understand without a legend.

**Keep it honest.** Document what you found, including the uncomfortable findings. If a system is in poor health, say so. If the data quality is bad, quantify it. If the integration landscape is fragile, explain the risk.

**Keep it current.** Current state documentation has a shelf life. Systems change, people move, contracts expire. Date your documentation and plan to review it if the project extends beyond six months.

**Make it accessible.** Store the documentation where the team can find it. Use formats that don't require specialist tools to read. Write in plain language that non-technical stakeholders can understand.

The test of good current state documentation is whether it changes decisions. If your future state design would be the same whether or not you'd done the current state assessment, either the assessment was unnecessary (unlikely) or it wasn't thorough enough (more likely).

workedExample.title: Assessing DESNZ's Legacy Estate for Modernisation
workedExample.context: DESNZ has commissioned a current state assessment of its energy scheme management systems as the first phase of a modernisation programme. The department manages 12 energy schemes (grants, incentives, and regulatory compliance) through a mix of systems built over the past 15 years. The programme board wants to understand the current landscape before committing to a modernisation approach.
workedExample.approach:
The SA leads a six-week current state assessment with a small team.

**Weeks 1-2: System discovery and mapping.**
The team identifies 12 primary systems, but investigation reveals 23 additional supporting systems — databases, reporting tools, file shares, and spreadsheets — that weren't in any system register. Three systems are running on infrastructure that the department doesn't own (a previous contractor's cloud account). Two systems have no source code available — the original supplier went out of business.

**Weeks 3-4: Integration and data assessment.**
The integration map reveals 47 system-to-system connections, of which only 19 are documented. The remaining 28 are a mix of database links, file transfers, and manual processes. Data quality assessment of the three largest databases reveals: 15% duplicate records, 8% records with missing mandatory fields, and inconsistent use of reference data across systems.

**Week 5: Capability and debt assessment.**
Capability mapping reveals that 'process grant applications' — the core capability — is implemented differently in each scheme, with no shared components. Technical debt assessment identifies: 4 systems on unsupported operating systems, 6 systems using end-of-life frameworks, 2 systems with known security vulnerabilities that can't be patched without breaking functionality.

**Week 6: Synthesis and reporting.**
The SA produces a current state report with a clear executive summary: 'The current landscape is fragile, poorly documented, and expensive to maintain. The biggest risks are: (1) security vulnerabilities in systems that can't be patched, (2) dependency on infrastructure the department doesn't control, (3) data quality issues that undermine policy analysis. The biggest opportunity is: consolidating common capabilities across schemes to reduce duplication and improve consistency.'
workedExample.outcome: The current state assessment fundamentally changed the modernisation approach. The original plan was to replace all 12 systems with a single platform over three years. The assessment revealed that this was too risky — the integration complexity, data quality issues, and undocumented dependencies made a big-bang replacement extremely dangerous. Instead, the programme adopted a phased approach: (1) address immediate security risks, (2) establish shared components for common capabilities, (3) migrate schemes to the shared platform one at a time, starting with the simplest.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The current state was significantly worse than anyone expected. Without the assessment, the modernisation programme would have been planned based on an optimistic view of the landscape and would have encountered the real complexity during delivery — when it's most expensive to deal with. The six weeks invested in assessment saved an estimated 6-12 months of delivery delays and £2-3m in unplanned rework.

civilServiceScenario.title: The System Nobody Understands
civilServiceScenario.background: During a current state assessment for a DESNZ modernisation programme, you discover a critical system that processes payments for the Renewable Heat Incentive (RHI) scheme. The system was built eight years ago by a contractor who is no longer engaged. The source code is available but poorly documented. The system processes £200m in payments annually. The operations team can keep it running but cannot make changes to it. The last person who understood the system's internals left the department two years ago.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: This system is a critical dependency for the modernisation programme — it can't be replaced immediately because of the payment processing complexity, but it can't be left as-is because it's a significant operational and security risk. You need to assess the system's health, understand its dependencies, and recommend an approach.
constraints: The system processes £200m in payments annually — any disruption has immediate financial impact
No one in the department fully understands the system's internals
The source code is available but poorly documented with no automated tests
The system runs on an operating system that reaches end-of-life in 18 months
The original contractor is no longer available
The system has integrations with banking systems, HMRC, and the RHI application system
There is no disaster recovery capability — if the system fails, recovery is manual and could take weeks
Budget for addressing this system must come from the modernisation programme budget
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect responsible for assessing this system and recommending an approach to the programme board.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests your ability to assess a high-risk legacy system and communicate the risk to non-technical decision-makers. The key challenge is balancing urgency (the system is a significant risk) with pragmatism (it can't be replaced quickly because of its complexity and criticality).

Your assessment should cover: what the system does (functional mapping), how it does it (technical assessment), what depends on it (dependency mapping), what could go wrong (risk assessment), and what options exist for managing the risk (options appraisal). The recommendation will likely involve a combination of immediate risk mitigation (disaster recovery, security patching) and longer-term replacement planning.

practiceArtefact.description: For the RHI payment system scenario, produce a concise current state assessment that covers: system overview, technical health assessment, dependency map, risk register, and recommended approach. The assessment should be understandable by non-technical programme board members.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Focus on what the programme board needs to know to make decisions. They don't need to understand the technical details — they need to understand the risks, the options, and the costs. Use a traffic light system (red/amber/green) for health indicators. Quantify risks where possible (financial impact, probability, timeline).
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**RHI Payment System — Current State Assessment**

**Executive Summary:**
The RHI payment system is a critical but fragile component processing £200m annually. It has no disaster recovery, runs on soon-to-be-unsupported infrastructure, and cannot be modified by the current team. Immediate action is needed to mitigate operational risk while a replacement is planned.

**System Overview:**
- Purpose: Calculates and processes quarterly payments to RHI scheme participants
- Users: 8 caseworkers (internal), ~15,000 payment recipients (indirect)
- Technology: .NET Framework 4.5, SQL Server 2014, Windows Server 2012 R2
- Built: 2016 by [Contractor], no longer engaged
- Code: Available, ~120,000 lines, minimal documentation, no automated tests

**Health Assessment:**
- Infrastructure: RED — OS end-of-life in 18 months, database version unsupported
- Security: RED — 3 known vulnerabilities, cannot be patched without regression risk
- Maintainability: RED — No one understands the internals, no tests, poor documentation
- Reliability: AMBER — Currently stable but no DR capability
- Performance: GREEN — Handles current volumes adequately

**Dependencies:**
- Upstream: RHI application system (receives approved claims)
- Downstream: Banking system (BACS payments), HMRC (tax reporting), Finance system (reconciliation)
- Data: Holds 8 years of payment history (~2TB)

**Risk Register:**
| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| System failure with no DR | Medium | Critical (£200m payments disrupted) | Implement DR capability (£150k, 3 months) |
| Security breach via known vulnerabilities | Medium | High (financial and reputational) | Network isolation + WAF (£50k, 1 month) |
| OS end-of-life (18 months) | Certain | High (no security patches) | OS upgrade or migration (£200k, 6 months) |
| Key person dependency | High | Medium (cannot make changes) | Knowledge capture and documentation (£100k, 3 months) |

**Recommended Approach:**
Phase 1 (Immediate, 0-3 months): Implement disaster recovery, apply network-level security controls, begin knowledge capture through code analysis.
Phase 2 (Short-term, 3-12 months): Migrate to supported infrastructure, establish automated testing, document system behaviour.
Phase 3 (Medium-term, 12-24 months): Replace with modern payment processing capability as part of the wider modernisation programme.

Estimated cost: Phase 1: £300k, Phase 2: £400k, Phase 3: included in modernisation programme budget.

reflectiveQuestions: How well do you understand the current state of the systems you work with? Could you draw an accurate system map from memory?
When was the last time you discovered a system or integration that nobody had told you about? How did it affect your project?
How do you communicate technical debt to non-technical stakeholders? What analogies or frameworks do you use?
Think about a pain point that users or operators have reported. Have you traced it to its root cause, or are you treating the symptom?
How honest is your current state documentation? Does it describe reality or an idealised version of reality?

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is current state assessment considered a risk mitigation activity?
options: Because it produces documentation that satisfies governance requirements
Because understanding the current landscape prevents expensive surprises during delivery
Because it delays the start of development, giving the team more time to plan
Because it identifies which systems should be decommissioned
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Current state assessment prevents expensive surprises by revealing integration complexity, data quality issues, technical debt, and dependencies before you commit to a design. Every hour spent understanding the current state saves multiple hours of rework during delivery.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most common cause of government IT project delays related to current state?
options: Budget overruns due to unexpected costs
Integration with legacy systems that behave differently from documentation
Staff turnover during the project
Changes in ministerial priorities
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Legacy system integration is the most common source of delays because legacy systems frequently behave differently from their documentation (or have no documentation). Interfaces that were assumed to work in a certain way turn out to have undocumented quirks, limitations, or dependencies.

knowledgeCheck.question: When documenting the current state, you discover that a critical system has significant security vulnerabilities. What should you do?
options: Document it in the current state report and move on — it's not your system to fix
Fix the vulnerabilities immediately before continuing the assessment
Document the risk with its potential impact and escalate it to the appropriate risk owner immediately, while continuing the assessment
Omit it from the report to avoid alarming stakeholders
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Security vulnerabilities in critical systems require immediate escalation to the risk owner (typically the SIRO or system owner) because they represent an active risk. Document the finding in your assessment and escalate it separately — don't wait for the final report. But don't try to fix it yourself; that's the system owner's responsibility.

knowledgeCheck.question: What distinguishes a pain point from a root cause?
options: Pain points are reported by users; root causes are identified by architects
Pain points are symptoms that people experience; root causes are the underlying issues that create those symptoms
Pain points are technical issues; root causes are organisational issues
There is no meaningful difference — they're the same thing described differently
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Pain points are the symptoms people experience ('the system is slow,' 'we can't get the data we need'). Root causes are the underlying issues that create those symptoms (inefficient queries, poor data architecture, missing data sharing agreements). Addressing root causes eliminates symptoms; addressing symptoms without fixing causes leads to recurring problems.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is capability mapping more useful than system mapping alone?
options: Because capability maps are easier to create than system maps
Because capabilities include people and process dimensions, not just technology, giving a richer picture of what needs to change
Because system maps are too technical for non-technical stakeholders
Because the GDS Service Manual requires capability maps but not system maps
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Capability mapping considers people, process, and technology together. When you replace a system, you're changing a capability — and if you only understand the technology dimension, you'll miss the people and process changes that are equally important for success.

practicalExercise.title: Conducting a Mini Current State Assessment
practicalExercise.scenario:
You've been asked to assess the current state of DESNZ's environmental reporting systems as preparation for a consolidation programme. You know the following:
- System A: Collects air quality data from 150 monitoring stations (built 2018, cloud-hosted, REST APIs)
- System B: Manages waste reporting from 5,000 businesses (built 2012, on-premises, file-based integration)
- System C: Tracks water quality compliance (built 2008, on-premises, no API, manual data entry)
- All three systems feed data to a central reporting database that produces ministerial briefings
- The reporting database was built by a contractor who left 3 years ago
practicalExercise.task:
1. Create a system landscape diagram (described in text) showing the four systems and their connections
2. Identify the top 5 risks in this landscape
3. Assess each system's health using a Red/Amber/Green rating across four dimensions: infrastructure, security, maintainability, and integration capability
4. Recommend priorities for the consolidation programme based on your assessment
hints: Consider the age of each system and what that implies for the technology stack
Think about the reporting database as a critical dependency — what happens if it fails?
Consider the different integration patterns — REST API vs file-based vs manual — and what that means for consolidation
Think about which system poses the greatest risk and which offers the greatest opportunity
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**System Landscape:**
System A (Air Quality, 2018) --[REST API]--> Reporting Database
System B (Waste Reporting, 2012) --[File Transfer/SFTP]--> Reporting Database
System C (Water Quality, 2008) --[Manual CSV Upload]--> Reporting Database
Reporting Database --[Manual Queries]--> Ministerial Briefings

150 monitoring stations --> System A
5,000 businesses --> System B (file upload)
Manual data entry operators --> System C

**Top 5 Risks:**
1. Reporting database is a single point of failure with no documented knowledge — if it fails, ministerial briefings stop
2. System C (2008) is likely running on unsupported infrastructure with potential security vulnerabilities
3. No one understands the reporting database internals — changes and fixes are impossible
4. Manual data entry in System C introduces data quality risks and is not scalable
5. File-based integration with System B is fragile — no error handling, no retry, no monitoring

**Health Assessment:**
| System | Infrastructure | Security | Maintainability | Integration |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| System A (2018) | GREEN | GREEN | AMBER | GREEN (REST APIs) |
| System B (2012) | AMBER | AMBER | AMBER | AMBER (file-based) |
| System C (2008) | RED | RED | RED | RED (manual only) |
| Reporting DB | AMBER | AMBER | RED | RED (no API, manual queries) |

**Recommended Priorities:**
1. **Immediate:** Assess and mitigate security risks in System C and the reporting database. Implement basic monitoring and backup for the reporting database.
2. **Short-term:** Replace System C with a modern service that has API capability, addressing the highest-risk system first.
3. **Medium-term:** Modernise the reporting database with proper API access, automated reporting, and documented architecture.
4. **Longer-term:** Upgrade System B's integration from file-based to API-based. System A is healthy and can be integrated into the consolidated platform last.

Rationale: Prioritise by risk (System C and reporting DB are highest risk) rather than by opportunity (System A is easiest to consolidate but lowest risk).
assessmentCriteria: System landscape accurately represents the systems and their connections
Risks are specific, prioritised, and connected to evidence from the assessment
Health assessment uses consistent criteria and is justified by the system characteristics
Recommendations prioritise by risk rather than by ease of implementation

commonMistakes: Skipping current state assessment because you're eager to start designing the future state
Relying on existing documentation without validating it against reality
Only mapping the systems within your project scope, ignoring the wider landscape
Treating pain points as root causes and designing solutions that address symptoms
Producing current state documentation that's too technical for decision-makers to use
Being dishonest about the current state to avoid political discomfort
Underestimating integration complexity — the connections between systems are often harder to change than the systems themselves
Ignoring shadow IT and informal processes that fill gaps between formal systems

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA reviews the existing architecture documentation, accepts it as accurate, and starts designing the future state. During development, the team discovers three undocumented integrations, a database with 15% duplicate records, and a critical system running on unsupported infrastructure. Each discovery causes delays, rework, and budget overruns. The programme is six months late and £1.5m over budget.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA spends six weeks conducting a thorough current state assessment. They discover the undocumented integrations, the data quality issues, and the infrastructure risks before design begins. The future state design accounts for these realities — including data migration complexity, integration rework, and infrastructure upgrades. The programme delivers on time because the plan was based on reality, not assumptions.

workplaceSignals: You can draw an accurate system map of your current landscape from memory, including the informal systems and workarounds
Your current state documentation is referenced by the team during design and delivery, not filed and forgotten
You've identified and escalated risks in the current landscape before they became incidents
You can explain the technical debt in your systems to non-technical stakeholders using language they understand
Your future state designs explicitly address current state constraints and risks
You've discovered systems, integrations, or data issues that weren't in any existing documentation
You distinguish between pain points and root causes, and your recommendations address causes
Your current state assessments have changed the approach or timeline of programmes based on what they revealed
